overview: Libya is a large country in North Africa, on the Mediterranean coast. Its capital and largest city is Tripoli. Libya became independent in 1951. It has the largest proven oil reserves in Africa. Since the overthrow of Muammar Gaddafi in 2011, the country has been split between rival governments.

geography.text: About 90 percent of Libya is desert, part of the Sahara, with sand seas and rocky plateaus. Most people live along the Mediterranean coast, especially around Tripoli and Benghazi. Libya has no permanent rivers; a huge network of pipes called the Great Man-Made River carries water from underground reserves in the desert to the coast.

history.text: Greeks founded Cyrene in the east and Phoenicians settled the west in ancient times, and the region later became part of Rome. After Arab and Ottoman rule, Italy invaded in 1911. Libya became independent in 1951 as a kingdom. Muammar Gaddafi seized power in 1969 and ruled until he was overthrown in 2011; the country has been divided since.

events.title: Italian invasion
events.text: Italy takes Libya from the Ottomans.

events.title: Gaddafi
events.text: Muammar Gaddafi takes power in a coup.

government.text: Libya has been divided since the civil war that followed Muammar Gaddafi's overthrow in 2011. A UN-recognised government is based in Tripoli in the west, while a rival administration backed by Khalifa Haftar's forces controls the east. National elections have been repeatedly delayed.

economy.text: Libya has Africa's largest proven oil reserves, and oil makes up almost all of its exports and government income. Fighting has often disrupted production.

culture.text: Libya has some of the best-preserved Roman cities in the world, such as Leptis Magna and Sabratha. Most of the country is Sahara desert. Ghadames, an oasis town of covered alleyways, is a UNESCO site.

items.title: Leptis Magna
items.text: A Roman city with a theatre facing the sea.

sport.text: Football is the most popular sport, and Libya hosted the Africa Cup of Nations in 1982, finishing second.
